content: The treatment regimen was designed in alignment with the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations. The use of linezolid was evaluated based on evidence that focused on a regimen including bedaquiline, levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, ethionamide, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, high-dose isoniazid, clofazimine, and pyrazinamide. Secondary analyses of longer regimens containing both bedaquiline and linezolid demonstrated favorable outcomes when these two agents were included together. The rationale for adding linezolid was to safeguard the regimen, particularly bedaquiline, while awaiting susceptibility test results for additional resistance to fluoroquinolones and other drugs. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) decided that until new evidence becomes available on shorter regimens that include both bedaquiline and linezolid, the recommended all-oral shorter regimen containing bedaquiline should not include linezolid. However, the group encouraged countries to consider using a modified all-oral regimen containing both bedaquiline and linezolid under operational research conditions until further evidence is available. A patient-centered approach is essential, requiring efforts to provide adequate support to ensure full adherence to treatment. The implementation of this regimen necessitates routine drug susceptibility testing (DST) not only for patient selection but also for monitoring the development of drug resistance. Although no major safety risks were identified in the data reviewed, active tuberculosis (TB) drug safety monitoring and management systems must be in place to rigorously monitor adverse events and promptly detect, manage, and report suspected or confirmed drug toxicities. The GDG identified several research priorities to address gaps in evidence for managing multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB). These include studies comparing all-oral shorter regimens containing bedaquiline and linezolid with other companion drugs, studies assessing these regimens in specific subgroups such as pregnant or lactating women, randomized controlled trials or operational research to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of shorter regimens, investigations into mechanisms of resistance acquisition to bedaquiline and genetic markers for resistance, and efforts to standardize data collection to contribute to global recommendations. The Nix-TB study, conducted by the TB Alliance, was a phase three, open-label, prospective cohort study assessing the safety, efficacy, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of a six-month treatment regimen comprising bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL), extendable to nine months for patients with missed doses or persistent culture positivity. The study enrolled 108 patients with extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) or MDR/RR-TB who were treatment-intolerant or non-responsive to previous regimens. Patients were followed for up to 24 months post-treatment completion. The BPaL regimen included pretomanid at 200 mg once daily, bedaquiline at 400 mg daily for the first two weeks followed by 200 mg three times weekly, and linezolid at an initial dose of 1200 mg daily. Close microbiologic, clinical, and adverse event monitoring was integral to the study. The study demonstrated high success rates but also highlighted significant adverse events, particularly related to linezolid, with 32% of patients discontinuing the drug due to toxicity. The GDG noted the high success rates of the Nix-TB study but acknowledged the uncertainty of the evidence, reflected in a very low certainty rating. The panel evaluated the desirable effects of the shorter regimen as moderate, considering the reduced treatment burden compared to longer regimens. However, concerns about adverse events, particularly with linezolid, and the need for further evidence on the regimen's safety and effectiveness were emphasized. Additional data reviewed by the GDG included cost-effectiveness analyses, acceptability studies, pharmacokinetic modeling, and preclinical and early clinical data on pretomanid. These analyses were sponsored by the TB Alliance and informed the development of recommendations for the BPaL regimen. The GDG highlighted the need for further research to refine and optimize treatment strategies for MDR/RR-TB and XDR-TB patients.
